lines.trans: Chef, where has our big stove disappeared to?
I personally took it to a reliable repair service.
But it was working perfectly yesterday evening!
I turned it in for important preventive maintenance.
And on what are we to cook today?
For now cook the dishes on this little hotplate.
This little hotplate heats up much too slowly!
Stop whining, cooks must know how to do everything!
The guests will wait for their orders very long!
Set the heat to four and get to work!
When will they return our old stove to us?
In a day or two they will bring everything!

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('so, and what about') (starting a question: а жвачку?) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Declinable neuter noun meaning 'dish', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('platter') (large flat serving dish) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Настоящий повар чувствует каждый вкус блюда.
examples.trans: A real chef feels every taste of the dish.

examples.text: Осталось ровно три минуты до готовности блюда.
examples.trans: Exactly three minutes remain until the dish is ready.
The chef prepared a delicious dish.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('big, large').

examples.text: Аракелян просит время. Сумма очень большая.
examples.trans: Arakelyan is asking for more time. The sum is very large.

meanings.note: the present tense is normally left out: я мэр = I am the mayor
Secondary conversational sense ('there is, there are') (present есть; у меня есть = I have) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
future: буду / будешь ... + infinitive

examples.trans: You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('important').

examples.text: Я тебе утром говорил: не торопись. Это очень важный вопрос.
examples.trans: I told you this morning: don't rush. It's a very important question.

вернуть.gloss: to give back, to get back

meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to give back', forming an aspectual pair with 'возвращать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to get back') (money you spent) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ты эти деньги через полгода вернёшь.
examples.trans: You'll get this money back in six months.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
до вечера = until the evening; вечером = in the evening
Secondary conversational sense ('party, evening event') (e.g. a school evening) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Добрый вечер, Вика. С Новым годом!
examples.trans: Good evening, Vika. Happy New Year!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'yesterday'.

examples.text: Я вчера ел маринованные грибы. Может, один гриб был плохой.
examples.trans: Yesterday I ate pickled mushrooms. Maybe one mushroom was bad.

meanings.note: Abstract masculine noun formed with the productive Slavic suffix '-ость', denoting the quality or state of 'guest'.

examples.trans: All the guests love them very much.

examples.text: Сегодня вечером к нам придут гости.
examples.trans: Guests are coming to our place tonight.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to prepare') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: 'два' with masculine/neuter nouns, 'две' with feminine; the noun goes into the genitive singular

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели. Я решу все ваши проблемы.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: He talks for a long time.
We'll make it! The president always talks for a long time.

meanings.note: + infinitive; agrees with the subject: должна (f)
Secondary conversational sense ('owe') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Жадность, Паша, должна быть умеренная. Комнатной температуры.
examples.trans: Greed, Pasha, should be moderate. Room temperature.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to wait', forming an aspectual pair with 'подождать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to expect') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'order', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('booking') (commission or reservation) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я делаю всё точно по вашему заказу.
examples.trans: I do everything exactly according to your order.
In the kitchen they are preparing this order.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'or', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.
Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'when'.

examples.trans: When I grow up, I'll be the mayor.

examples.text: Когда ты наконец принесёшь горячий соус на раздачу?
examples.trans: When will you finally bring the hot sauce to the pass?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'where'.

examples.trans: Wait, where are you two going?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Аникеев лично сюда приезжал, и что?
examples.trans: Anikeev came here in person, and what?

examples.text: Пятнадцать лет мы просим новое здание! Аникеев лично сюда приезжал, и что?
examples.trans: For fifteen years we've been asking for a new building! Anikeev came here in person, and what?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('small, little').
Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'heating', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Поставьте нагрев на четвёрку и работайте!
examples.trans: Set the heat to four and get to work!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'греваться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to heat up', forming an aspectual pair with 'нагреться'. The reflexive suffix '-ся'/'-сь' makes the action intransitive, reciprocal, or directed at the subject.

examples.text: Эта маленькая плитка нагревается слишком медленно!
examples.trans: This little hotplate heats up much too slowly!

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (stem 'дёжный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('reliable').

examples.text: Она не очень надёжная. Я бы не рекомендовал.
examples.trans: She's not very reliable. I wouldn't recommend her.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'but', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to whine'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Хватит ныть, повара должны уметь всё!
examples.trans: Stop whining, cooks must know how to do everything!

examples.text: Хватит ныть, у меня хорошее настроение.
examples.trans: Quit whining, I am in a good mood.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('she') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

отвезти.gloss: to drive, to take (someone somewhere by vehicle)

meanings.en: to take, to drive (someone to a place)
meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'везти'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to drive, to take (someone somewhere by vehicle)', paired with 'отвозить'.

examples.trans: Afterwards I'll drive you back for free.

examples.text: Вот это дело! Потом обратно бесплатно отвезу.
examples.trans: Now we're talking! Afterwards I'll drive you back for free.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'excellently'.
Secondary conversational sense ('great!, excellent!') (as a one-word reply) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I know this town really well!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'stove', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('slab') (large flat stone or concrete block) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Внимательно смотри за температурой на плите.
examples.trans: Watch carefully the temperature on the stove.

examples.text: Я сниму сковороду с горячей плиты вовремя.
examples.trans: I will remove the pan from the hot stove on time.

examples.text: Ладно, включай плиту и доставай мясо!
examples.trans: All right, turn on the stove and get the meat!

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'hotplate'.

examples.text: Пока готовьте блюда на этой плитке.
examples.trans: For now cook the dishes on this little hotplate.

examples.text: Эта маленькая плитка нагревается слишком медленно!
examples.trans: This little hotplate heats up much too slowly!

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'for now'.
Secondary conversational sense ('while') (as a conjunction: пока я сплю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('bye, see you') (informal goodbye) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ладно, ребята, всем пока, увидимся завтра утром на смене!
examples.trans: All right, guys, bye everyone, see you tomorrow morning on shift!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ставить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to put', forming an aspectual pair with 'ставить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to install') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Put your foot on the bed.

examples.text: Заходите. Поставьте, пожалуйста, правую ногу на кровать.
examples.trans: Come in. Please put your right foot on the bed.

meanings.note: from a trip, by car, train or plane

examples.trans: Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'пасть'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to disappear, vanish'.

examples.text: Аркадий, что делать будем? Самсонов пропал.
examples.trans: Arkady, what are we going to do? Samsonov is missing.

examples.text: Таня, а куда пропал твой бывший муж?
examples.trans: Tanya, and where did your former husband disappear to?

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'prevention'.

examples.trans: The stove was taken for maintenance.

examples.text: Я сдал её для важной профилактики.
examples.trans: I turned it in for important preventive maintenance.

meanings.note: работать + instrumental = to work as: работать мэром

examples.text: Я уже четыре года работаю мэром.
examples.trans: I've been working as mayor for four years now.

сдать.gloss: to return, to hand in; to pass (an exam)

meanings.en: to return, to hand back, to turn in
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'дать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to return', forming an aspectual pair with 'сдавать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to pass') (an exam: сдать экзамен) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нам надо сдать машину до десяти часов.
examples.trans: We have to return the car before ten o'clock.

examples.text: Я за комнаткой пригляжу. Может, сдам кому, а денежки пополам!
examples.trans: I'll look after the little room. Maybe I'll rent it to someone, and we'll split the money!

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.text: Виктор Степанович, сегодня никак не могу.
examples.trans: Viktor Stepanovich, I really can't today.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'repair shop', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Я лично отвёз её в надёжный сервис.
examples.trans: I personally took it to a reliable repair service.

examples.text: Я просто переживаю за вечерний сервис.
examples.trans: I am simply worried about the evening service.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лишком').

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'old', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('former, old') ('старый друг' = an old friend) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Славик, смотри сюда. Меняю свой новый айфон на твой старый телефон.
examples.trans: Slavik, look here. I'll swap my new iPhone for your old phone.

уметь.gloss: to know how to, to be able to

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'меть'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to know how to', forming an aspectual pair with 'суметь'.

examples.text: Эх, Паша, Паша. Ты считать не умеешь.
examples.trans: Oh, Pasha, Pasha. You can't count.

meanings.note: impersonal, + genitive: денег не хватило = there wasn't enough money
Secondary conversational sense ('that's enough!') (хватит!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Gum? I didn't have enough money.

examples.text: Хватит спорить из-за пустяков, давайте лучше спокойно работать!
examples.trans: Enough arguing over trifles, let us just work calmly instead!

meanings.note: + accusative: через неделю = in a week
Secondary conversational sense ('through, across') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нормально? Она через неделю снова потечёт!
examples.trans: Fine? It'll be leaking again in a week!

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'four'.

examples.text: Поставьте нагрев на четвёрку и работайте!
examples.trans: Set the heat to four and get to work!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') whose case form reflects its grammatical role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('that') (conjunction) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('? = well?') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
